title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
abstract: Large pre-trained language models store factual knowledge in their parameters, but their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is limited. We explore a general-purpose fine-tuning recipe for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that combines parametric memory with non-parametric memory. The retriever is a dense passage retriever (DPR) and the generator is a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model (BART). RAG models are evaluated on a wide range of knowledge-intensive NLP tasks, including open-domain question answering, and can generate more specific, diverse, and factual language than a state-of-the-art parametric-only seq2seq baseline.
demo_notes: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines a parametric sequence-to-sequence generator with a non-parametric dense index. The retriever is Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR), which embeds questions and passages with separate BERT encoders and retrieves the top-k passages by maximum inner product search. The generator is BART-large, a pretrained encoder-decoder. The retrieved passages are concatenated with the input question and passed to BART. Two formulations are studied: RAG-Sequence, which uses the same retrieved document for the whole output sequence, and RAG-Token, which can use different documents for different output tokens. The model is trained end-to-end by marginalizing over retrieved documents using the top-k approximation. Experiments cover Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTrec, MS MARCO, and Jeopardy. RAG obtains state-of-the-art results on three open-domain QA tasks and produces more factual and specific generations. The paper also analyzes the limitations: retrieval is fixed to Wikipedia, the retriever is not updated during generation, and end-to-end joint training can be expensive.

title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
abstract: We explore how large language models can generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner. ReAct prompts models to produce verbal reasoning traces and actions, allowing them to induce, track, and update action plans, handle exceptions, and gather external information. Experiments on HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld, and WebShop show improvements in interpretability, factuality, and task success over reasoning-only or acting-only baselines.
demo_notes: ReAct interleaves thought, action, and observation steps. In each step the model writes a natural-language thought, selects an action such as Search or Lookup, receives an observation from the environment, and continues. On knowledge-intensive tasks the actions call a Wikipedia API and the model combines evidence across multiple hops. On HotpotQA and FEVER, ReAct improves factuality and reduces hallucination compared with chain-of-thought prompting alone, while being more interpretable because the reasoning trace is explicit. On interactive decision-making benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning baselines by a large margin with only a few in-context examples. The authors also discuss failure modes: the model can repeat actions, get stuck in loops, or fail to recover when the retrieved observation is irrelevant. ReAct is a foundational design for modern tool-calling agents.

title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
abstract: We show that language models can teach themselves to use external tools via simple APIs in a self-supervised way. Toolformer decides which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to incorporate the results. The approach is evaluated with a calculator, a question answering system, a machine translation system, a calendar, and a Wikipedia search engine, improving zero-shot performance on several downstream tasks without sacrificing language modeling ability.
demo_notes: Toolformer uses a self-supervised pipeline: for each API, it samples candidate API calls at possible positions in a large text corpus, executes them, and keeps a call only if the resulting text has a lower language-modeling loss than the original text. The filtered calls are used to fine-tune the model to insert API calls and use their outputs. The APIs include a calculator, a question-answering system, a machine translation system, a calendar, and a Wikipedia search engine. Toolformer improves zero-shot performance on arithmetic, QA, multilingual tasks, and temporal reasoning. The paper also shows that the model can decide not to call a tool when it is unnecessary. Limitations include dependence on the quality of the loss heuristic and the fixed set of APIs.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
abstract: We introduce Self-RAG, a framework that enhances language model quality and factuality through retrieval and self-reflection. Self-RAG trains a single language model to adaptively retrieve passages on demand and to generate self-reflection tokens that critique its own output. Reflection tokens include whether retrieval is needed (Retrieve), whether a passage is relevant (ISREL), whether a claim is supported (ISSUP), and whether the response is useful (ISUSE). Experiments on diverse tasks show improvements over strong retrieval-augmented baselines.
demo_notes: Self-RAG uses reflection tokens to make retrieval and generation adaptive. The model first predicts a Retrieve token to decide whether retrieval is needed. If retrieval is needed, it retrieves passages and generates candidate continuations. It then predicts ISREL to judge passage relevance, ISSUP to judge whether the generated claim is fully or partially supported by the passage, and ISUSE to judge overall response usefulness. At inference, a segment-level beam search uses these critic scores to select the best continuation. The critic is trained with data generated by a stronger model and human annotations. Self-RAG improves factuality, citation accuracy, and long-form generation quality on PopQA, TriviaQA, PubHealth, ARC-Challenge, and biography generation. Unlike standard RAG, which always retrieves and does not critique evidence, Self-RAG can skip retrieval and reject unsupported claims.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
abstract: We show that dense representations can be used for open-domain question answering retrieval, outperforming a strong sparse BM25 system by a large margin. We use a simple dual-encoder architecture with separate BERT encoders for questions and passages, trained with a contrastive objective. The key is to train the encoders with a small number of positive passages and a large number of negative passages, including in-batch negatives. The resulting DPR retriever substantially improves retrieval and end-to-end QA performance.
demo_notes: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) uses a dual-encoder architecture: a question encoder and a passage encoder, both initialized from BERT. The similarity is the dot product of the two embeddings, and retrieval is maximum inner product search over a passage index. Training data for each question includes one or more positive passages and a set of negative passages. The paper compares random negatives, BM25 negatives, and in-batch negatives, and finds that combining BM25 negatives with in-batch negatives works best. In-batch negatives are especially efficient because all passages in a mini-batch serve as negatives for other questions. DPR is evaluated on Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, and CuratedTrec. With the same reader, DPR improves top-20 retrieval accuracy from 59.1 to 78.4 on WebQuestions and improves end-to-end exact match. DPR is later reused as the retriever in RAG.

title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
abstract: We present ColBERT, a passage search model that introduces a late interaction paradigm. ColBERT encodes queries and passages independently with BERT, keeps token-level embeddings, and computes relevance using a fast maximum similarity operation. This preserves the efficiency of independent encoding while capturing fine-grained term interactions. ColBERT is competitive with state-of-the-art BERT-based rankers while being orders of magnitude faster.
demo_notes: ColBERT introduces late interaction. Queries and documents are encoded separately by BERT into token-level embedding matrices. Relevance is computed with MaxSim: for each query token, find the maximum dot product with any document token, then sum these maxima. This is more expressive than a single-vector dual encoder but much cheaper than cross-encoder full attention over the pair. ColBERT uses a token-level embedding compression and a vector index for candidate retrieval. On MS MARCO and TREC CAR, it improves over strong baselines while being much faster than BERT cross-encoders. The paper shows that late interaction retains fine-grained matching signals, such as term importance and proximity, and that a larger number of query/document tokens improves quality at some storage cost.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
abstract: We analyze how language models use long contexts through two controlled experiments: multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval. Performance is often highest when relevant information appears at the beginning or end of the context and degrades significantly when it is in the middle, producing a U-shaped curve. This behavior persists in state-of-the-art models and has implications for retrieval-augmented generation and long-context applications.
demo_notes: The paper studies whether language models actually use information placed in long input contexts. In multi-document QA, the relevant document is placed at different positions among many distractors. Accuracy is highest when the relevant document is first or last and drops when it is in the middle, creating a U-shaped curve. A similar pattern appears in a synthetic key-value retrieval task. The authors evaluate open models, proprietary models, and models with extended context windows. They find that extended context models do not eliminate the position bias. The work motivates careful ordering of retrieved evidence, reranking, and context compression in RAG pipelines. It also warns that simply increasing the context window is not a substitute for retrieval quality.

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: We explore chain-of-thought prompting, where a model is prompted with a few exemplars that show intermediate reasoning steps. This simple method substantially improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. Experiments on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning benchmarks show that chain-of-thought prompting scales with model size and can outperform standard prompting by a large margin.
demo_notes: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting provides few-shot exemplars that include intermediate natural-language reasoning steps before the final answer. The method is evaluated on arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, MAWPS), commonsense reasoning (CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA), and symbolic reasoning (last letter concatenation, coin flip). CoT improves performance most for large models: with PaLM 540B it reaches 56.9 percent solve rate on GSM8K, compared with 17.9 percent for standard prompting. The paper shows that reasoning ability emerges at sufficient scale, and that CoT is relatively robust to exemplar choice. It does not help small models much and can produce fluent but incorrect reasoning chains.

title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is effective for local questions but struggles with global questions that require understanding an entire corpus. We propose Graph RAG, which builds a knowledge graph from source documents, partitions it into a hierarchy of communities, generates summaries for each community, and uses these summaries to answer query-focused summarization questions. Graph RAG improves comprehensiveness and diversity over naive RAG on global sensemaking tasks.
demo_notes: Graph RAG addresses query-focused summarization over a corpus. It uses an LLM to extract entities, relationships, and claims from source documents, builds a knowledge graph, and applies community detection to form hierarchical communities. For each community it generates summaries at different levels. At query time it uses map-reduce style partial answers from community summaries, then reduces them into a final answer. This design supports global questions such as what are the main themes in the corpus, which naive chunk retrieval cannot answer well because no single chunk contains the global picture. The paper evaluates on podcast transcripts and news datasets, and reports improvements in comprehensiveness and diversity. Costs include LLM calls for graph construction and summarization.

title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is sensitive to the quality of retrieved documents. We propose Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG), which uses a lightweight retrieval evaluator to assess the quality of retrieved documents and trigger corrective actions. Depending on the confidence, CRAG can refine the retrieved knowledge, decompose the question, or perform web search. Experiments show improved robustness and generation quality.
demo_notes: CRAG adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator that assigns a confidence score to retrieved documents. Based on the score it selects one of three actions: Correct for high confidence, Incorrect for low confidence, and Ambiguous for uncertain cases. Correct refines the retrieved knowledge into finer-grained strips and filters irrelevant parts. Incorrect discards the retrieved documents and performs web search. Ambiguous combines internal knowledge with web search results. The method is plug-and-play with different RAG pipelines and generators. It improves robustness on short-form and long-form generation tasks, especially when the retriever returns noisy or irrelevant documents. Limitations include the cost of external web search and reliance on the evaluator's calibration.
